title: The publish attestation proves which workflow minted the token, not which code ran in it — so malware in the test phase ships a perfectly attested release
index_line: T-0081 · EXEC · PR-target cache poisoning → OIDC token lifted from the runner → attested malicious npm publish that self-propagates · node · corroborated
invariant_violated: The registry's trust decision was 'did this token come from the publisher's release workflow?'. A token can be minted by any code executing in that workflow, including code the attacker got run during a test or cleanup step — provenance attested the pipeline identity, not the code identity.

mechanism.does: a fork pull request drives a pull_request_target workflow, so attacker-influenced code executes with the base repository's privileged context
the job poisons the shared GitHub Actions cache across the fork/base trust boundary, carrying the payload into the trusted job
during the test phase the payload runs and extracts a live OIDC token from the runner process memory (the workflow holds id-token: write)
the registry accepts the token because it is bound to the legitimate workflow file/ref (trusted publisher), not to the step that minted it
the defined publish step was skipped (tests had failed) but the crafted publish call goes straight to the registry, so 84 versions across 42 packages appear
installing an affected version resolves a malicious optionalDependency whose prepare lifecycle script runs a credential harvester that republishes every package the victim maintains

source.env.value: the CI runner: workflow permissions, the shared Actions cache, and a mintable OIDC id-token

guard.signature.value: the registry's trusted-publisher/OIDC attestation — a proof of pipeline identity that says nothing about which code ran

delegate.tool.value: npm's prepare lifecycle: the package manager runs the dependency's install-time script on the developer's machine

sink.exec.shell.value: the install-time script executes attacker code (obfuscated router_init.js) with the developer's credentials in reach

preconditions.expr: the release workflow uses id-token: write with pull_request_target and a shared cache
a published version of the package carries an install-time script that is not in the upstream sources

check.spec: npm view PKG@VERSION scripts dist.tarball time --json 2>/dev/null | head -40

preconditions.expr: consumers install with lifecycle scripts enabled

success: a published version's tarball contains a prepare/postinstall script that fetches or decodes an external payload
the registry records the publish as provenance-attested from the legitimate workflow while the workflow's own publish step did not run
failure_like: the workflow requires environment approval on the OIDC-gated job, so test-phase code cannot mint the token
the registry rejects publishes from steps other than the declared one, or install scripts are disabled
false_positive: a package with legitimate postinstall scripts is normal — the signal is a script absent from the repository at the published tag, or a version published outside the workflow's own publish step
a provenance badge alone does not certify content; do not treat attestation as a clean bill of health

hazards: any CI that mints short-lived publish/deploy tokens with the same job that runs untrusted code
cache poisoning crosses build matrices and jobs, so the poisoned artefact appears in the trusted job
self-propagation: the payload harvests the victim's own registry credentials and republishes their packages, so the blast radius is the maintainer graph
non_transfers: workflows that mint publish tokens only in a protected environment after tests pass
install-time scripts disabled across the fleet

provenance.author: StepSecurity (Ashish Kurmi)
provenance.corroborates: detected and analysed the incident: 84 malicious versions of 42 @tanstack/* packages, self-spreading credential harvester, npm ecosystem propagation

provenance.author: TanStack (incident postmortem)
provenance.corroborates: root cause: pull_request_target Pwn Request + GitHub Actions cache poisoning across the fork/base boundary + runtime memory extraction of an OIDC token, publishing via the OIDC trusted-publisher binding for release.yml although the defined publish step was skipped; install-time prepare script harvests credentials and republishes every package the victim maintains
